title: Pasado simple / Simple past (regular and irregular verbs)
bridge: In German, the simple past (Präteritum) is used almost exclusively in writing and narratives, whereas in conversation the present perfect (Perfekt) is preferred. Unlike Spanish, where the simple past is common in everyday speech, in German you must recognize the Präteritum for reading and writing, but when speaking you will use the Perfekt more often. Additionally, modal verbs and the auxiliaries sein and haben are used in Präteritum in spoken language, which can be confusing. Note that regular verbs add -te, while irregular verbs change their vowel.
rule: To form the Präteritum of regular verbs, take the verb stem and add -te, followed by the personal endings: -, -st, -, -n, -t, -n. Example: machen (to do) → ich machte, du machtest, er machte, wir machten, ihr machtet, sie machten. Irregular verbs change their vowel in the past and often do not take -te; their endings are: -, -st, -, -en, -t, -en. Example: gehen (to go) → ich ging, du gingst, er ging, wir gingen, ihr gingt, sie gingen. Modal verbs (können, müssen, etc.) and auxiliaries (sein, haben) form their Präteritum irregularly and are common in conversation. Präteritum is not used to express a completed past action in general, but rather for narration or expressing states. Exceptions: mixed verbs like bringen (to bring) → brachte, or denken (to think) → dachte, which combine vowel change and the -te ending.

concept_examples.translation: Yesterday I did my homework.
He used to walk every day.
We didn’t have time.
She could swim well.

common_error.correct_alt: Ich habe gestern meine Hausaufgaben gemacht.
common_error.explanation: In German, the past participle (gemacht) is only used with the auxiliary haben to form the present perfect, which goes at the end of the sentence. To use the simple past, you must conjugate the verb in Präteritum (machte). Spanish speakers tend to use the construction with the past participle because in Spanish the simple past is formed with a single word, but in German you must remember that the Präteritum has its own conjugated form.

examples.translation: I used to play the piano.

Ending -test for du. Remember that in the du form, -test is added.

title: Präsens mit gerundivischer Bedeutung / Continuous Present
bridge: In Spanish, to express an ongoing action we use the periphrasis 'estar + gerund' (estoy comiendo). In German, there is no equivalent compound verbal form: the simple present (Präsens) is used without an auxiliary. This can be confusing because while Spanish differentiates between 'como' (I eat) and 'estoy comiendo' (I am eating), in German both ideas are expressed with the same form 'ich esse'. Additionally, German often adds adverbs like 'gerade' (right now) to specify that the action is happening at this moment.
rule: German does not have a specific verb tense for the continuous present. The present form (Präsens) covers both the simple present and the continuous present, depending on the context. To emphasize that an action is in progress, time adverbs such as 'gerade' (right now), 'jetzt' (now), 'im Moment' (at the moment) or constructions with 'am + infinitive + sein' (colloquial, especially in northern Germany: 'Ich bin am Arbeiten') are used. In standard language, it is most common to use the present and the context or the adverb to communicate progression. Basic rule: if in Spanish you would say 'estar + gerund', in German use the present (conjugated) and, if you want to be more specific, add 'gerade'.

concept_examples.translation: I am eating (right now).

concept_examples.text: Sie arbeitet im Moment im Garten.
concept_examples.translation: She is working in the garden at this moment.
concept_examples.phonetic: ziː ˈaʁbaɪ̯tət ɪm moˈmɛnt ɪm ˈɡaʁtn̩

concept_examples.translation: We are playing soccer.
I am reading a book.

common_error.explanation: Spanish speakers often try to translate 'estar + gerund' literally by using 'sein' + present participle. In German, the present participle (essend) is not used with the verb 'sein' to form a continuous tense. It is an ungrammatical construction. The correct form is to use the simple present. The colloquial alternative 'am + substantivized infinitive + sein' ('Ich bin am Essen') exists and is valid in everyday speech, but it is not suitable for all registers and is often considered regional (northern Germany). For an A2 student, the safest option is to use the simple present and, if you want to be more specific, add 'gerade'.

examples.note: The simple present in German expresses the ongoing action. There is no morphological mark of the progressive.
'gerade' se coloca después del verbo conjugado y refuerza el matiz de acción en curso.
'gerade' is placed after the conjugated verb and reinforces the nuance of an ongoing action.

examples.note: This structure is widely used in colloquial speech (especially in northern Germany) to express progression. 'am' is combined with the substantivized infinitive (capitalized).

title: Future with 'werden' / Future with 'going to'
bridge: In Spanish, to express a planned or intentional future, we use 'ir a + infinitive' (e.g., 'voy a comer'). In German, the equivalent structure is 'werden + infinitive' (e.g., 'ich werde essen'). Unlike Spanish, in German the verb 'werden' is conjugated irregularly and always appears in second position in the main clause, while the infinitive goes at the end. Caution: do not confuse 'werden' with 'würden' (conditional), which is used for hypothetical situations.
rule: The future in German (Futur I) is formed with the auxiliary verb 'werden' conjugated according to the person and the infinitive of the main verb at the end of the sentence. The conjugation of 'werden' in the present tense is: ich werde, du wirst, er/sie/es wird, wir werden, ihr werdet, sie/Sie werden. It is used to express intentions, plans, predictions, or assumptions about the future. It is common in written and formal language; in colloquial speech, the present tense with a time adverb (e.g., 'morgen' or 'bald') is often used to refer to the future. In normal word order sentences, the auxiliary goes in second position, and the infinitive at the end: 'Ich werde morgen nach Madrid fliegen.' In subordinate clauses (with 'dass', 'wenn', etc.), the conjugated verb (werden) goes at the end: 'Ich glaube, dass ich morgen Zeit haben werde.' The verb 'werden' is also used for the passive voice, but in that case it is accompanied by a past participle, not an infinitive.

concept_examples.translation: I am going to learn German tomorrow.
Are you going to travel this weekend?
We are going to eat later.

common_error.wrong: Ich werde morgen fliegen nach Berlin.
common_error.correct: Ich werde morgen nach Berlin fliegen.
common_error.correct_alt: Morgen werde ich nach Berlin fliegen.
common_error.explanation: In German, the infinitive verb (here 'fliegen') must go at the end of the main clause, not after the place object. Spanish speakers tend to place the verb closer to the subject, as in 'voy a volar a Berlín'. To avoid this, remember the structure: subject + conjugated werden + additional information + infinitive at the end.

examples.translation: I am going to read the book.
examples.note: The auxiliary 'werden' is conjugated (ich werde) and the infinitive ('lesen') goes at the end.

examples.translation: You are going to receive a gift.
examples.note: Note the irregular form 'du wirst' (not 'werdest').

examples.translation: She is going to call soon.
examples.note: 'Sie wird' can mean 'she' or 'usted' (formal).

examples.translation: Are you going to cook tonight?
examples.note: In yes/no questions, the verb 'werden' goes first.

examples.translation: What are we going to do tomorrow?
examples.note: With an interrogative pronoun, 'werden' goes in second position after the question.

examples.translation: Who is going to close the window?
examples.note: The question word 'wer' (who) is the subject and goes before the verb.

examples.original: Ich glaube, dass ich morgen Zeit habe.
examples.phonetic: [ɪç ˈɡlaʊ̯bə das ɪç ˈmɔʁɡən tsaɪ̯t ˈhaːbə]
examples.translation: I think I will have time tomorrow.
examples.note: In subordinate clauses with 'dass', the conjugated verb goes at the end. Here the present tense is used with future meaning, which is common.

examples.original: Er sagt, dass er kommen wird.
examples.note: In the subordinate clause, 'wird' goes at the end, after the infinitive 'kommen'.

examples.original: Wenn wir Glück haben, werden wir das Spiel gewinnen.

examples.translation: If we are lucky, we will win the game.
examples.note: The conditional clause with 'wenn' uses the present tense; the main clause uses 'werden' to express the future.

title: Futur I (Simple Future)
bridge: In Spanish, to express the future we use the endings -é, -ás, -á... (hablaré, comerás) or the periphrasis 'ir a + infinitive'. In German, there are no special endings for the future: the auxiliary verb 'werden' (which means 'to become') is used, conjugated according to the person, and the main verb in the infinitive at the end of the sentence. The trick: 'werden' is an irregular verb, and its position in the sentence is crucial — the auxiliary goes in second position (like a conjugated verb) and the infinitive goes at the end, which does not happen in Spanish.
rule: To form the simple future (Futur I) in German, use the auxiliary verb 'werden' conjugated in the present tense, followed by the infinitive of the main verb at the end of the sentence. The conjugations of 'werden' are: ich werde, du wirst, er/sie/es wird, wir werden, ihr werdet, sie/Sie werden. The basic structure is: [Subject] + [conjugated werden] + ... + [Infinitive]. In subordinate clauses, the conjugated verb (werden) also goes at the end. It is not used to express an immediate intention as much as in Spanish; for that, the present tense is often used (Ich gehe morgen nach Berlin). But for talking about predictions, assumptions, or future plans, Futur I is appropriate.

title: Komparativ and Superlativ / Comparatives and Superlatives
bridge: In Spanish, we form comparatives with 'más... que' and superlatives with 'el más...'. In German, the comparative is formed with '-er' and 'als' is used for 'que' (not 'wie'). The superlative is formed with 'am -sten' when it is predicative and with 'der/die/das -ste' when it is attributive. Be careful with umlauted vowels (Umlaut) in some adjectives and with exceptions like 'gut', 'viel', 'gern'.
rule: In German, the comparative of adjectives is formed by adding '-er' to the base form: 'schnell' -> 'schneller'. The comparison is introduced with 'als' (equivalent to 'que' in Spanish): 'Er ist schneller als ich' (He is faster than me). Do not use 'wie' for superiority comparisons, only for equality ('so... wie'). The predicative superlative is formed with 'am' + adjective + '-sten' (or '-esten' if it ends in -d, -t, -s, -x, -z): 'am schnellsten' (the fastest). The attributive superlative is formed with 'der/die/das' + adjective + '-ste' (or '-este'): 'der schnellste Zug' (the fastest train). Many one-syllable adjectives take an umlaut (ä, ö, ü) in the comparative and superlative: 'alt' -> 'älter' -> 'am ältesten'. Common exceptions: 'gut' -> 'besser' -> 'am besten', 'viel' -> 'mehr' -> 'am meisten', 'gern' -> 'lieber' -> 'am liebsten'.

title: Modalverben: müssen, sollen, dürfen, können, wollen, mögen / Modal verbs
bridge: In Spanish, modal verbs function as conjugated verbs followed by an infinitive (debo hacer, puedo hacer, quiero hacer). In German, modals are also conjugated, but they occupy the second position in the sentence, with the main verb at the end in the infinitive. Additionally, unlike Spanish, German modals have special present tense forms for 'ich' and 'er/sie/es' (e.g., 'ich muss', 'er muss') that do not follow the regular pattern. Be careful with 'müssen' (obligation) and 'sollen' (recommendation or mandate from others), which are often confused because in Spanish both can be translated as 'deber'.
rule: The modal verbs in German are: müssen (to have to), sollen (should, recommendation), dürfen (may, permission), können (can, ability), wollen (to want), and mögen (to like, to want in an affectionate sense). In the present tense, they are conjugated as follows: ich muss/soll/darf/kann/will/mag, du musst/sollst/darfst/kannst/willst/magst, er/sie/es muss/soll/darf/kann/will/mag, wir müssen/sollen/dürfen/können/wollen/mögen, ihr müsst/sollt/dürft/könnt/wollt/mögt, sie/Sie müssen/sollen/dürfen/können/wollen/mögen. In a declarative sentence, the conjugated modal goes in the second position, with the main verb in the infinitive at the end: 'Ich muss heute arbeiten.' (I have to work today). In questions, the modal comes first: 'Muss ich das machen?' (Do I have to do that?). To negate, use 'nicht' after the modal or before the infinitive: 'Ich kann nicht kommen.' (I cannot come). Modals do not take 'zu' with the infinitive. In the past tense, the Präteritum is used (musste, sollte, durfte, konnte, wollte, mochte), and in the perfect tense, it is formed with 'haben' + double infinitive: 'Ich habe gehen müssen' (I had to go). For A2 level, it is important to master the present tense and constructions with the infinitive at the end.

You should drink more water (they recommend it).
We are not allowed to smoke here.
Can you help me?

common_error.explanation: In Spanish, a question can be formed simply with intonation ('¿Yo tengo que ir a trabajar mañana?'), but in German inversion is mandatory: the conjugated modal verb must come first. Additionally, in an affirmative sentence, the modal goes in the second position; if you place it at the end, the structure is incorrect. Remember: in questions, the modal comes first.

title: Reflexive verbs / Reflexive verbs
bridge: In Spanish we use reflexive verbs like 'lavarse' or 'sentirse', and German also has them, but with important differences. First, the reflexive pronoun in German has its own forms for 'mich' (me), 'dich' (you), 'sich' (him/her/it/themselves), etc., and its use does not always match that of Spanish reflexives. For example, 'ich freue mich' means 'I am happy', but 'sich freuen' is not always translated literally as 'to be happy' in all contexts. Additionally, some verbs are reflexive in German but not in Spanish, such as 'sich erinnern' (to remember, not 'recordarse'). Watch out for these false reflexive friends!
rule: Reflexive verbs in German are conjugated with a reflexive pronoun in the accusative (mich, dich, sich, uns, euch, sich) or dative (mir, dir, sich, uns, euch, sich) depending on the verb. Most use the accusative, but some, like 'sich etwas ansehen' (to look at something), use the dative for the indirect object. The reflexive pronoun comes after the conjugated verb, or after the subject if it is a pronoun. In main clauses, the reflexive pronoun goes right after the verb: 'Ich wasche mich' (I wash myself). In subordinate clauses, it comes after the subject. Some common A2 reflexive verbs include: 'sich freuen' (to be happy), 'sich interessieren für' (to be interested in), 'sich anziehen' (to get dressed), 'sich ausruhen' (to rest). Not all Spanish reflexive verbs have a reflexive equivalent in German, and vice versa. For example, 'quedarse' is translated as 'bleiben' (not reflexive), and 'sich bemühen' (to make an effort) is reflexive in German but not in Spanish. In the imperative, the reflexive pronoun is placed after the verb: 'Wasch dich!' (Wash yourself!). With modal verbs, the reflexive pronoun goes at the end: 'Ich muss mich beeilen' (I have to hurry up).

In German, 'sich erinnern' is reflexive and requires 'an + accusative'. The confusion arises because in Spanish 'recordar' is not reflexive (yo recuerdo algo), while in German it is 'sich erinnern' (me acuerdo). To avoid this, memorize verbs that are reflexive in German even if they are not in Spanish, such as: sich erinnern (to remember), sich treffen (to meet), sich ausruhen (to rest).

title: Object pronouns / Direct and indirect object pronouns
bridge: In Spanish, direct (lo, la, los, las) and indirect (le, les) object pronouns are relatively easy to distinguish by context and are often placed before the verb. In German, however, you need to learn four cases (nominative, accusative, dative, and genitive), and pronouns change depending on the case. Direct object pronouns go in the accusative case (mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch, sie), while indirect object pronouns go in the dative case (mir, dir, ihm, ihr, uns, euch, ihnen). A common mistake is using the same pronoun for both cases, as in Spanish, but in German you must choose the correct form based on the grammatical function.
rule:
Direct (accusative) and indirect (dative) object pronouns in German have distinct forms for each person. For A2 level, you should memorize the basic forms:

**Accusative (direct object):** mich (me), dich (you), ihn (him), sie (her), es (it), uns (us), euch (you all), sie (them).

**Dative (indirect object):** mir (me), dir (you), ihm (him), ihr (her), ihm (it), uns (us), euch (you all), ihnen (them).

**Placement rule:** The object pronoun is generally placed before the conjugated verb in main clauses, or after the auxiliary verb if there is a past participle or infinitive. In sentences with two objects, the indirect object pronoun (dative) usually comes before the direct object pronoun (accusative), similar to Spanish, but with pronouns, both always come before the verb: "Ich gebe ihm es" (I give it to him) is incorrect; the correct form is "Ich gebe es ihm" (I give it to him).

**Common dative-governing verbs:** gefallen (to like), helfen (to help), danken (to thank), antworten (to answer), gehören (to belong). With these verbs, the indirect object is mandatory.

**Common accusative-governing verbs:** haben (to have), sehen (to see), lieben (to love), kaufen (to buy), etc.

**Important:** In sentences with two pronouns, the accusative comes before the dative. This differs from the order with nouns, where the dative comes before the accusative.

**Exception:** In questions or emphatic phrases, the order may vary, but for A2 level, stick to the standard order.

He helps me.
We give them the book.
Can you give it to me?

common_error.explanation: In Spanish, the direct object pronoun 'te' is the same for subject and object in some colloquial constructions, but in German, the subject 'du' (you) must change to the accusative form 'dich' when it is a direct object. Spanish speakers often confuse subject and object forms because in Spanish, 'tú' is sometimes used instead of 'te' in informal contexts, but in German, using the correct case form is mandatory.

'euch' is the accusative pronoun for 'ihr' (you all).
The verb 'helfen' requires the dative case, so 'mir' (me) is used instead of 'mich'.

When there are two pronouns, the accusative (es) comes before the dative (ihm). In Spanish, the indirect object usually comes first, but in German, with pronouns, it is the opposite.

title: Adverbien der Häufigkeit / Frequency adverbs
bridge: En español, los adverbios de frecuencia suelen colocarse antes del verbo (ej. 'siempre como') o al final. En alemán, su posición es más fija: normalmente van después del verbo conjugado en oraciones principales (posición 2 del verbo). Además, en alemán hay adverbios específicos como 'manchmal' (a veces) que no tienen equivalente directo en español (a veces vs. algunas veces). Presta atención a la inversión cuando el adverbio se coloca al inicio de la oración.
rule: Frequency adverbs in German indicate how often an action occurs. The most common ones are: immer (always), meistens (usually), oft (often), manchmal (sometimes), selten (rarely), nie (never). In a main clause, the conjugated verb is in second position, and the frequency adverb is placed immediately after the verb. In clauses with modal or auxiliary verbs, the adverb goes after the modal/auxiliary and before the infinitive or past participle. If the adverb is placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis, inversion occurs: the verb comes before the subject. Unlike Spanish, 'nie' is not combined with 'nicht' (no double negation). Example: 'Ich gehe nie ins Kino' (I never go to the cinema), not 'Ich gehe nicht nie...'.

concept_examples.text: Ich trinke immer Kaffee am Morgen.
concept_examples.translation: I always drink coffee in the morning.

examples.translation: I am often in the park.
examples.note: With the verb 'sein', the adverb also comes after the conjugated form.
'Selten' is placed after the verb, not at the end as in Spanish.

examples.translation: Can you visit your parents often?

title: Zeitpräpositionen: am, um, im / Time prepositions: am, um, im
bridge: In Spanish, we use 'en', 'a', or 'por' for many time expressions (en marzo, a las tres, por la mañana). In German, these ideas are divided among 'im' (months, seasons), 'am' (days, parts of the day), and 'um' (hours). The main trap: in Spanish we say 'en la mañana', but in German it's 'am Morgen' (not 'in der Morgen'). Additionally, months and seasons are masculine in German, so they always take 'im'.
rule: In German, the most common time prepositions are 'im', 'am', and 'um'. 'Im' is used with months (im Januar), seasons (im Sommer), and years (im Jahr 2024). 'Am' is used with days of the week (am Montag), specific dates (am 5. Mai), and parts of the day (am Morgen, am Abend) except for night, which is 'in der Nacht'. 'Um' is used only with exact times (um 8 Uhr) and specific moments like noon or midnight (um Mittag, um Mitternacht). No preposition is used with 'heute', 'morgen', 'gestern', or 'jeden' (jeden Tag). Remember that days are masculine, but 'am' merges the preposition 'an' with the article 'dem'.

To avoid this error, remember: day = am, time = um, month/season = im.

title: Conjunctions (and, but, or, because, if, when)
bridge: In German, conjunctions like 'und' (and), 'aber' (but), and 'oder' (or) are used similarly to Spanish, but be careful with word order. Subordinating conjunctions such as 'weil' (because), 'wenn' (when/if), and 'als' (when, for past events) send the conjugated verb to the end of the clause. This is very different from Spanish, where the verb usually comes after the subject. For example: 'Weil ich müde bin' (Because I am tired) – the verb 'bin' goes at the end. Another key point: 'wenn' is used for conditions and repeated events in the present/future, while 'als' is used for a single past event. In Spanish, both are often confused with 'cuando'.
rule: Coordinating conjunctions (und, aber, oder, denn) do not change the word order. The structure is: Subject + Verb + ... + Conjunction + Subject + Verb + ... (example: 'Ich gehe, aber du bleibst'). 'Denn' is a coordinating conjunction meaning 'because' and does not alter the word order. Subordinating conjunctions (weil, wenn, als, dass, ob) send the conjugated verb to the end of the subordinate clause. The structure is: Main clause + Conjunction + Subject + ... + Conjugated Verb at the end. Example: 'Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil es regnet.' (I stay at home because it is raining). 'Wenn' is used for conditions ('if') and for 'when' in the present or future (repeated or habitual events). 'Als' is used for 'when' in the past, referring to a single, specific event. The difference is crucial: 'Wenn ich Zeit habe' (When I have time) vs. 'Als ich Kind war' (When I was a child). Remember that in German, a comma separates the subordinate clause from the main clause.

But in German, with 'weil', the conjugated verb ('arbeite') must go at the end of the clause. Additionally, the adverb 'viel' (a lot) must come before the verb. title: Perfekt – Present perfect tense
bridge: In Spanish, you use the present perfect (he comido) for recent actions or those with present relevance. In German, the Perfekt is also widely used in conversation for the past, but it is formed differently: with an auxiliary verb (haben or sein) and the past participle at the end of the sentence. Unlike Spanish, where the auxiliary is simply 'haber', German chooses between 'haben' and 'sein' depending on the verb. Additionally, in German, the past participle does not follow the auxiliary as in Spanish—it goes at the end of the sentence, which is a significant change in word order.
rule: The Perfekt is used to express past actions, especially in spoken and colloquial language. It is formed with the present tense of the auxiliary verbs 'haben' or 'sein' + the past participle (Partizip II) of the main verb, which is placed at the end of the sentence. The choice of auxiliary depends on the verb: 'sein' is used with intransitive verbs of movement or change of state (gehen, kommen, fahren, werden, sterben), as well as verbs like 'bleiben' and 'sein'. For most other verbs, 'haben' is used (including transitive, reflexive, and modal verbs). Formation of the participle: regular verbs: ge- + stem + -t (machen -> gemacht); irregular verbs: ge- + stem (often with vowel change) + -en (gehen -> gegangen); verbs with inseparable prefixes (be-, ver-, ent-, etc.) do not take 'ge-' (besuchen -> besucht); verbs ending in -ieren do not take 'ge-' (studieren -> studiert). In main clauses, the conjugated verb (auxiliary) is in second position, and the participle is at the end. Example: 'Ich habe das Buch gelesen.' (I have read the book). For questions and subordinate clauses, the word order varies.

He has gone to Berlin.
We have seen the movie.
Did you arrive yesterday?

common_error.explanation: The error occurs because it is assumed that all verbs use 'haben' as in Spanish 'he fahrado'. In German, movement verbs like 'fahren' (to go) require the auxiliary 'sein'. The general rule: use 'sein' with verbs that indicate a change of place or state, especially with intransitive movement verbs. Always ask: does the verb indicate movement or transformation? If so, it likely uses 'sein'.

title: Imperativ: Commands and Prohibitions / Imperative: Orders and Prohibitions
bridge: In Spanish, we use the imperative to give orders (¡habla!, ¡hablad!, ¡hablen!). In German, the form changes depending on who you are addressing: one person (du), multiple people (ihr), or formally (Sie). A typical mistake made by Spanish speakers is always using the 'usted' form or mixing the persons. Remember: in the informal imperative for 'du', verbs with vowel changes (e->i) keep that change (du sprichst -> sprich!), and verbs ending in -ern or -eln may drop the final -e. Additionally, the informal imperative does not use the pronouns 'du' or 'ihr', except in the formal 'Sie' form, which comes after the verb.
rule:
The German imperative has three main forms:

1. **Informal form for 'du'**: Formed from the verb stem in the present tense (second person singular) without the -st ending. For regular verbs, -e is added (optional but more common in written language): 'du gehst' -> 'Geh!' or 'Gehe!' (Go!). Verbs with vowel changes e->i or e->ie: keep the change and do not use -e: 'du sprichst' -> 'Sprich!' (Speak!), 'du liest' -> 'Lies!' (Read!). Verbs ending in -d, -t, -ig, -m, -n usually add -e for euphony: 'Antworte!' (Answer!), 'Öffne!' (Open!). Verbs ending in -eln/-ern may drop the final -e: 'Lächle!' or 'Läch(e)le!' (Smile!).

2. **Informal form for 'ihr'**: Uses the present tense form for 'ihr' without the pronoun: 'ihr geht' -> 'Geht!' (Go! - vosotros). No additional ending is added.

3. **Formal 'Sie' form**: Uses the infinitive + 'Sie' (after the verb): 'Gehen Sie!' (Go, please!), 'Sprechen Sie bitte langsam!' (Speak slowly, please!).

**Negation**: 'nicht' is placed after the object or adverb: 'Sprich nicht so laut!' (Don’t speak so loudly!), 'Gehen Sie nicht!' (Don’t go!).

**Separable verbs**: the prefix separates and goes at the end: 'Komm rein!' (Come in!), 'Räum dein Zimmer auf!' (Tidy up your room!).

**Irregular verbs**: sein -> 'Sei!' (Be!), 'Seid!' (Be! - vosotros), 'Seien Sie!' (Be! - formal); haben -> 'Hab!' (Have!), 'Habt!' (Have! - vosotros), 'Haben Sie!' (Have! - formal).

Usage: to give instructions, orders, advice, recipes, directions. At A2 level, mastery of the forms for 'du', 'ihr', and 'Sie', and their negation is expected.

Go home now!
Please take a seat!
Eat your vegetables!

common_error.explanation: The error occurs because in Spanish we often use the conjugated form with a pronoun to give orders (¡hablas! sometimes sounds softer), and we transfer that to German. In German, the informal imperative for 'du' is formed without a pronoun and without the -st ending. Do not use 'du' with the imperative (except in the formal 'Sie' form). For a softer request, use 'Kannst du bitte langsamer sprechen?' (Can you speak more slowly?).

Verb 'lesen' with e->ie change: 'lies' is used (without -e).
Verb ending in -nen: -e is added for easier pronunciation.
No pronoun 'ihr' and no additional ending.

With 'sein', negation also goes at the end.

title: Zählbare und unzählbare Nomen / Countable and uncountable nouns
bridge: In Spanish, the distinction between countable and uncountable nouns exists, but in German the grammatical mark is more visible: uncountable nouns do not have a plural form and are used without an indefinite article in the singular. For example, 'agua' in Spanish can colloquially say 'una agua', but in German 'Wasser' never takes an indefinite article. Another key point: countable nouns in German use 'ein/eine' in the singular, while uncountable nouns are used with 'viel' or 'wenig', never with 'viele'.
rule: In German, countable nouns (zählbare Nomen) can be pluralized and are combined with 'ein/eine' in the singular and with 'viele' in the plural. Uncountable nouns (unzählbare Nomen) have no plural form and are used without an article in the singular, with 'viel' or 'wenig'. Typical examples: 'das Wasser' (the water), 'die Milch' (the milk), 'der Reis' (the rice). You do not say 'ein Wasser' to refer to water in general, but 'ein Glas Wasser' (a glass of water). With countable nouns, 'viele' (many) and 'wenige' (few) are used with the plural, while with uncountable nouns 'viel' (much) and 'wenig' (little) are used. To express quantity of uncountable nouns, measures are used: 'ein Kilo Reis', 'eine Tasse Kaffee'.

concept_examples.translation: I bought a loaf of bread.
I drink a lot of water.
He has many apples.
I want a glass of milk.

common_error.explanation: In Spanish, 'mucho' can be used with both countable and uncountable nouns ('muchos libros', 'mucha agua'), but in German the distinction is mandatory: 'viel' is only for uncountable nouns and 'viele' for countable nouns in the plural. 'Bücher' is countable, so 'viele' is required.

examples.note: Countable nouns like 'Tisch' are used with 'ein/eine' in the singular.
Abstract concepts like 'Hunger' are uncountable and do not take an article.
Materials and substances like 'Zucker' are uncountable, they have no plural form.

levels.label: Mengenangaben: viel, wenig, viele, wenige
levels.translation: Expressions of quantity: much, little, many, few

examples.note: 'Zeit' is uncountable, so 'wenig' is used in the singular.
'Freunde' is a countable plural, so we use 'viele'.

examples.translation: He drinks a lot of coffee.
examples.note: Coffee as a substance is uncountable, so 'viel'.
To measure uncountable nouns like 'Reis', a unit like 'Kilo' is used.
The container is used as a measure: 'Flasche' for liquids.
The word 'Stück' (piece) is used to count portions of uncountables.

title: Algo y nada / Something and nothing (and their compounds)
bridge: In Spanish we use 'algo', 'nada', 'alguien', 'nadie', 'algún' and 'ningún' to express existence or absence. In German, these concepts are expressed with 'etwas' (something), 'nichts' (nothing), 'jemand' (someone), 'niemand' (no one), 'irgendein-' (some) and 'kein-' (no). Unlike Spanish, where 'no...nada' with double negation is often used, in German negation is expressed with 'nichts' or 'niemand' without adding an extra 'nicht'. Additionally, compounds with 'irgend-' (some) are used in affirmative statements to indicate indeterminacy, while in Spanish 'algo' or 'alguien' may be used simply.
rule:
In German, the following pronouns and adjectives are used to express indefinite quantities or existence:
- 'etwas' (something) for non-specific quantities, 'nichts' (nothing) for total negation.
- 'jemand' (someone) and 'niemand' (no one) for indefinite people.
- 'irgendein', 'irgendeine', 'irgendwelche' (some) for non-specific objects or people in affirmative statements.
- 'kein', 'keine', 'keinen' (no) before nouns to negate existence.
- Compounds with 'irgend-' (irgendetwas, irgendjemand, irgendwo) emphasize indeterminacy: 'irgendetwas' (anything), 'irgendjemand' (anyone), 'irgendwo' (somewhere).
- In negative sentences, 'nicht' is used to negate verbs, but to negate existence 'nichts', 'niemand' or 'kein-' are used without an additional 'nicht' (unlike Spanish, which uses double negation: 'no hay nada').
- Possessive and demonstrative adjectives agree with the noun; for example, 'kein' declines according to gender, number and case (kein, keine, keinen, etc.).

concept_examples.translation: Have you eaten something?
I haven’t said anything.
Can you see someone?

concept_examples.text: Es gibt keinen Stuhl im Zimmer.
concept_examples.translation: There isn’t any chair in the room.
concept_examples.phonetic: ɛs ɡiːpt ˈkaɪnən ʃtuːl ɪm ˈtsɪmɐ

common_error.explanation: Spanish speakers often transfer the double negation from Spanish ('no...nada') to German, saying 'nicht nichts' (not nothing). In German, double negation is incorrect; 'nichts' is simply used with a positive verb form to negate. Another option is to use 'kein' with the noun: 'kein Essen' (no food). It’s important to remember that in German negation is not cumulative: one negative form (nichts, niemand, kein-) is chosen instead of combining it with 'nicht'.

examples.note: 'etwas' is used for 'some' or 'something' in affirmative statements. It is often translated as 'some' with uncountable nouns.
'etwas' can be accompanied by a declined adjective as a noun (etwas Vergleichbares = something comparable).
'nichts' combines with 'zu + infinitive' to express 'nothing to do'.
No 'nicht' is added; the sentence is correct with just 'nichts'.
In questions, 'jemand' is common for 'someone'.
'Niemand' means 'no one' and is used alone, without 'nicht'.
Remember that 'jemand' declines: in accusative it is 'jemanden'.
'niemand' in accusative is 'niemanden'.
'irgendjemand' emphasizes that the person is unknown or irrelevant.
'irgendetwas' means 'something, anything'.
'kein' is used before nouns to negate existence.
'irgendwelche' is used for 'some' or 'any' in plural.

title: viel, viele, eine Menge / Much, many, a lot
bridge: In Spanish, 'mucho' changes according to gender and number, but in German it gets more complicated: you have 'viel' for uncountable nouns and 'viele' for countable plural nouns, plus 'eine Menge', which functions as a noun. A typical error is using 'viel' with countable plural nouns, like *'viel Bücher'*, when it should be 'viele Bücher'. Also, in German, 'viel' can be used as an adverb, and 'eine Menge' requires the preposition 'von' when followed by a plural noun.
rule: In German, 'viel' (much) is used with uncountable nouns or in singular, e.g., 'viel Wasser' (much water). 'Viele' (many) is used with countable plural nouns, e.g., 'viele Bücher' (many books). 'Eine Menge' (a lot) is used as a noun meaning 'a large quantity' and, if followed by a plural noun, it uses 'von': 'eine Menge von Büchern' (a lot of books). 'Viel' can also be used as an adverb: 'Ich lerne viel' (I learn a lot).

concept_examples.translation: I have a lot of time.
He has many friends.
We have a lot of work.
She drinks a lot of coffee.

common_error.explanation: The error occurs because in Spanish 'mucho' is used for both countable and uncountable nouns, but in German you must distinguish: 'viel' for uncountable and 'viele' for countable plural nouns. To say 'a large quantity of' with countable nouns, you can also use 'eine Menge' (without 'von' when the noun is plural and no specific quantity is mentioned, though it is more formal with 'von').

examples.translation: I have a lot of money.
examples.note: Money is uncountable in this use, so 'viel'.

examples.translation: She has a lot of patience.
examples.note: Patience is abstract and uncountable.
Countable plural, so 'viele'.
Possibilities are countable.
Countable plural.

examples.translation: I have a lot of books.
examples.note: Omitting 'von' is common in colloquial use, but 'eine Menge von' is also correct.

examples.translation: He has a lot of friends.
examples.note: 'Von' is often omitted.

examples.translation: She buys a lot of fruit.
examples.note: With uncountable nouns, 'eine Menge' also works.

title: Relative clauses: der, die, das / Relative clauses: who, which, that
bridge: In Spanish, we use 'que' for people and things, and sometimes 'quien' for people. In German, relative pronouns decline and change according to gender, number, and case, just like articles: 'der', 'die', 'das'. Additionally, in German, the verb in the relative clause goes at the end, which does not happen in Spanish. Be careful: the relative pronoun can be 'der' (masculine), 'die' (feminine or plural), and 'das' (neuter), and sometimes it takes a preposition.
rule: In German, the relative clause is introduced by a relative pronoun that agrees in gender and number with the noun it refers to, but the case depends on its function in the relative clause. For A2, we focus on the nominative and accusative cases. The forms are: masculine: 'der' (nom.), 'den' (acc.); feminine: 'die' (nom. and acc.); neuter: 'das' (nom. and acc.); plural: 'die' (nom. and acc.). The conjugated verb is placed at the end of the relative clause. Examples: 'Der Mann, der hier wohnt' (The man who lives here) – 'der' is the subject. 'Der Mann, den ich sehe' (The man whom I see) – 'den' is the direct object. For things, 'die' (fem.), 'das' (neuter), and 'der' (masc.) are also used; there is no separate equivalent of 'which'.

concept_examples.translation: The man who lives here is nice.
concept_examples.phonetic: deːɐ̯ man, deːɐ̯ hiːɐ̯ voːnt, ɪst nɛt

concept_examples.text: Die Frau, die ich kenne, kommt aus Spanien.
concept_examples.translation: The woman whom I know comes from Spain.
concept_examples.phonetic: diː fʁaʊ̯, diː ɪç ˈkɛnə, kɔmt aʊ̯s ˈʃpaːni̯ən

concept_examples.text: Das Buch, das auf dem Tisch liegt, ist neu.
concept_examples.translation: The book that is on the table is new.
concept_examples.phonetic: das buːx, das aʊ̯f deːm tɪʃ liːkt, ɪst nɔɪ̯

concept_examples.text: Die Kinder, die im Park spielen, sind glücklich.
concept_examples.translation: The children who are playing in the park are happy.
concept_examples.phonetic: diː ˈkɪndɐ, diː ɪm paʁk ˈʃpiːlən, zɪnt ˈɡlʏklɪç

common_error.wrong: Der Mann, wer hier wohnt, ist nett.
common_error.correct: Der Mann, der hier wohnt, ist nett.
common_error.explanation: In Spanish, 'quien' is sometimes used for people, but in German the relative pronoun is always 'der', 'die', or 'das', never 'wer' (which means 'who' in questions). To avoid this mistake, remember that the relative pronoun resembles the definite article: 'der, die, das'.

levels.label: Relativpronomen im Nominativ
levels.translation: Relative pronouns in the nominative case

examples.original: Der Mann, der hier arbeitet, ist mein Vater.
examples.phonetic: deːɐ̯ man, deːɐ̯ hiːɐ̯ ˈaʁbaɪ̯tət, ɪst maɪ̯n ˈfaːtɐ
examples.translation: The man who works here is my father.
examples.note: 'der' is the subject of the relative clause (nominative).

examples.original: Die Frau, die das Lied singt, ist berühmt.
examples.phonetic: diː fʁaʊ̯, diː das liːt zɪŋt, ɪst bəˈʁyːmt
examples.translation: The woman who sings the song is famous.
examples.note: 'die' refers to 'Frau' (feminine) and is the subject.

examples.original: Das Kind, das lacht, ist glücklich.
examples.phonetic: das kɪnt, das laxt, ɪst ˈɡlʏklɪç
examples.translation: The child who is laughing is happy.
examples.note: 'das' refers to 'Kind' (neuter).

levels.label: Relativpronomen im Akkusativ
levels.translation: Relative pronouns in the accusative case

examples.original: Der Mann, den ich sehe, ist alt.
examples.phonetic: deːɐ̯ man, deːn ɪç ˈzeːə, ɪst alt
examples.translation: The man whom I see is older.
examples.note: 'den' is the direct object, so it changes from 'der' to 'den'.

examples.original: Die Frau, die ich liebe, heißt Anna.
examples.phonetic: diː fʁaʊ̯, diː ɪç ˈliːbə, haɪ̯st ˈana
examples.translation: The woman whom I love is named Ana.
examples.note: 'die' remains the same in the accusative feminine.

examples.original: Das Buch, das ich lese, ist spannend.
examples.phonetic: das buːx, das ɪç ˈleːzə, ɪst ˈʃpanənt
examples.translation: The book that I am reading is exciting.
examples.note: 'das' does not change in the accusative neuter.

examples.original: Das ist der Mann, mit dem ich spreche.
examples.phonetic: das ɪst deːɐ̯ man, mɪt deːm ɪç ˈʃpʁɛçə
examples.translation: This is the man with whom I speak.
examples.note: The preposition 'mit' requires the dative case, so 'der' becomes 'dem'.

examples.original: Die Stadt, in der ich wohne, ist klein.
examples.phonetic: diː ʃtat, ɪn deːɐ̯ ɪç ˈvoːnə, ɪst klaɪ̯n
examples.translation: The city in which I live is small.
examples.note: The preposition 'in' takes the dative case, so 'die' becomes 'der'.

examples.original: Das Haus, in dem ich lebe, ist alt.
examples.phonetic: das haʊ̯s, ɪn deːm ɪç ˈleːbə, ɪst alt
examples.translation: The house in which I live is old.
examples.note: The preposition 'in' with the dative case changes 'das' to 'dem'.
